newsitem.title: USA: Texas town in shock after killer tornado.
newsitem.headline: Texas town in shock after killer tornado.

text.p: Rescue workers searched through the night on Wednesday for more victims of a deadly tornado that killed at least 30 people and left this small Texas town in a state of shock.

Survivors waited silently on Jarrell's dimly-lit main street for news of friends and families still missing in the twisted wreckage of dozens of homes destroyed by the storm that swept through on Tuesday afternoon.
Police wading in knee-deep mud called out for batteries to run heat-imaging devices they used to look for victims. At coffee breaks, they struggled for words to describe the scene.

"I've never seen anything in my entire law enforcement career this massive and this destructive. It's totally wiped clean... total, massive destruction," said Williamson County Constable Gary Griffin.

The tornado was one of six that struck central Texas in a spring storm that also brought torrential rains and baseball- sized hail. At least two other people died in Austin, 40 miles (62 km) to the south, including a man whose house was struck by a tornado and a girl who drowned in a rain-swollen creek, police said.

For the people of Jarrell, population 650, the tornado brought back memories of another twister that hit almost exactly eight years ago. But in that storm, only one person died. Tuesday's tornado was a force of nature they hoped never to witness again.
"This one sounded like a bear growling, low tones, an evil sound," said 17-year-old Danny Williams, who took refuge with father Billy Williams when the tornado passed near their home.
As soon as the tornado skipped away, they ran to the stricken area, pausing only long enough to take in the scene of flattened homes, broken trees and tossed-about cars.
"I thought: 'this must have been what Hiroshima looked like," said Billy Williams. "It looked like someone with a mile-wide plough went through and ploughed over a field."

They raced from the rubble of one house to another searching for survivors. The dead were badly mangled, their clothes ripped off and their skin burned by the deadly friction of 300 mile-per-hour (482 kph) winds.
"I knew these people and I could barely recognise them. It was hard to take. When I saw a dead little boy, I had to leave," said Billy Williams.
Deputy Constable Priscilla Smith said police found one woman holding a child who was wrapped in a blanket. Both were dead. "My stomach is still in knots about it," she said.
Along with the 30 people that police said were confirmed dead, rescue workers found dozens of dead cattle, dogs, horses and even an ostrich.
"I kept hearing gunshots going off and I couldn't figure out what it was. I realised later they were shooting animals who had been hurt," Smith said.

Police said as many as 50 houses and mobile homes were destroyed when the tornado ripped through Jarrell, which sits in rolling cattle country at the eastern edge of the Texas Hill Country. In all, about 200 buildings were damaged or destroyed across a four-county area by the six twisters.

Jimmy Wingo of the Morgan's Point Volunteer Fire Department on nearby Lake Belton said 310 boats were damaged by a tornado. "They're scattered from one end of the lake to the other. From what I've seen, it's mass chaos," he said.
The Jarrell dead were placed in a makeshift morgue in the city's small fire department. They were to be shipped to Austin for storage in the medical examiner's facility, police said.
Jarrell residents said they expected the death toll to rise as searchers picked through the rubble because several people were unaccounted for.
There were also fears that the storm's toll would rise as rescue workers delved into a tornado-damaged grocery store in the town of Cedar Park, Texas, just north of Austin.

Dogs were being used to search through the wreckage where one store worker was found in critical condition on Tuesday. Police said there were several unclaimed cars in the store's parking lot that may belong to victims.
